body:
Where Is Earth's Water?: 1. About 97 hold salt water; 3 hold fresh water. 2. Frozen in glaciers and ice caps: "About 2 of the 3 buckets would be frozen in glaciers and ice caps." 3. Water stored in soil and in tiny spaces between rocks underground. 4. When ocean water evaporates, the salt is left behind, so the water vapor and the rain it makes are fresh. 5. To make a huge amount of water easier to picture and compare: you can see that 97 out of 100 is almost all of it. 6. Main idea 1: most of Earth's water is salty or frozen, so very little is easy-to-use fresh water (detail: lakes, rivers and clouds fill only a few cupfuls). Main idea 2: the water cycle keeps making fresh water (detail: evaporation leaves the salt behind).
Explain the Water Cycle: The drawing labels evaporation (the sun warms water and it rises as vapor), condensation (the vapor cools into drops that form clouds), precipitation (drops fall as rain, snow or hail) and collection (water gathers in oceans, lakes, rivers and the ground), with arrows showing the cycle. A strong spoken explanation follows the steps in order, says what causes each one (the sun's heat; cooling as the vapor rises; drops getting heavy) and says how the cycle starts again.
Water Check: A strong explanation includes, in order: the sun warms the ocean and the drop evaporates into water vapor, leaving the salt behind; the vapor rises, cools and condenses into a cloud; the cloud moves over a mountain where it is cold, and the drop falls as snow (precipitation); the snow piles up and is pressed into glacier ice over many years (collection); later the ice melts, and the water flows downhill in a stream or river (runoff) back to the ocean. It is fresh because salt does not evaporate with the water.
Scoring tip: an explanation that names all four steps but never says what causes them is Developing on science; score organization on the order of the steps and the linking words, not on length.
title: Answer key: Earth's Water
